name: blink
why: A tiny x86-64 Linux emulator that lets you watch machine code execute, a strong door into how programs run.

brief.what_it_is: Blink is a user-mode x86-64 Linux emulator written in ANSI C11. It takes a Linux x86-64 ELF binary (or a Cosmopolitan Actually Portable Executable) and runs it on another POSIX host such as macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, or Cygwin, translating Linux system calls to the host. Its companion program, blinkenlights, is a terminal UI debugger that shows memory panels rendered as IBM Code Page 437 glyphs, which change as you step through the assembly. The README describes a headless blink mode and a blinkenlights TUI mode, and the TUI also supports reverse debugging by scrolling the mouse wheel over the assembly.
brief.why_it_exists: The README positions blink as a smaller, more portable alternative to qemu-x86_64: about 221kb versus a 4mb binary, running on any POSIX system rather than only Linux, and reportedly up to 2x faster on some benchmarks. Blinkenlights is framed as a visualization-first alternative to GDB: 'Unlike GDB, Blinkenlights focuses on visualizing program execution.'
brief.how_it_works: Instruction decoding uses a trimmed-down version of Intel's Xed disassembler. Hot code is JIT-compiled to native functions on x86_64 and aarch64, with the -j flag controlling JIT (the meaning is inverted between blink and blinkenlights). Guest memory is virtualized either through a four-level PML4T page table with a 16-entry TLB, or through a faster linear identity-mapped translation (disabled with -m), and Linux syscalls are emulated on top of the host OS.

Builds blink and blinkenlights in parallel using four jobs.

commands_seen.context: Installs the built programs system-wide; the README notes doas as a modern sudo replacement.
Prints version and build configuration to confirm the install.
Runs the bundled hello-world Cosmopolitan binary under Blink.
Runs the same hello-world binary under the blinkenlights debugger TUI.
Builds the smallest-footprint variant, which removes assertions and logging and is about 50% smaller.
Enables the emulated VFS so a full chroot'd Linux distro can run with correct absolute symlinks and /proc values, at some size and speed cost.
Runs Blink's local test suite of 700+ test programs.
Runs Actually Portable Python in the TUI with JIT and the linear memory optimization enabled, which the README says are needed for usable speed.

brief.install_notes: Build from source: needs a C11 compiler with atomics (GCC 4.9.4 or newer) and a modern GNU Make, not the one shipped with Xcode. No libraries beyond POSIX libc are required. The README's install path is ./configure, make, then doas make install, and blink -v plus man blink to verify. Blink downloads precompiled test binaries automatically, and make check2 / make emulates fetch static GCC and Qemu toolchains. The TUI needs a UTF-8 VT100/xterm-style terminal; recommended terminals include kitty, PuTTY, GNOME Terminal, and Terminal.app. Optional first-run files: blink writes blink.log in the current directory when something is logged, and BLINK_OVERLAYS can point at a root filesystem directory. Nothing in the README mentions Homebrew-specific steps beyond the brew formula, so I have no further detail on the brew install itself.
brief.standout: Blinkenlights turns execution into a visual experience: memory panels of CP437 glyphs animate as you single-step, and you can rewind execution history by scrolling backward over the disassembly. Blink's own claim is that it is a few hundred kilobytes and runs on far more hosts than qemu-user, which is unusual for an emulator.
brief.status: unknown. The README I read has no release dates, changelog, or commit history, and I did not follow the repository's releases or commits pages, so I cannot say whether it is actively maintained from what I saw. The README describes a long test regime (Cosmopolitan, LTP, and musl test suites) and a version string of blink-1.0, which is the only version hint.
brief.caveats: Not every Linux program works: the README says Blink returns EINVAL for many address families and Linux-only syscalls such as membarrier and System V message queues. x87 long double is not 80-bit; Blink uses 64-bit doubles. Some fringe instructions (BOUND, ENTER) are unimplemented, and most ring-0 instructions are unsupported. JIT exists only on x86_64 and aarch64 and only for 64-bit long-mode code. Running without JIT (-j in blink) is about 10x slower. Page-size mismatches on Apple M1 (16kb) and Cygwin (64kb) can produce an ELF p_vaddr error; the fix involves -m or relinking with -Wl,-z,max-page-size=65536. The debugger's -j and -m flags mean the opposite of the same flags in blink. MODE=tiny removes all assertions and logging, which the README says to use only if you are confident the build is bug-free for your use case. Debugging frames require -fno-omit-frame-pointer. License not stated in the README I read, so I cannot say what it is. The brew caveats field was empty.
quotes: blink is an x86-64 interpreter for POSIX platforms that's written in ANSI C11 that's compatible with C++ compilers.
Blink is 221kb in size (115kb with optional features disabled), whereas qemu-x86_64 is a 4mb binary.
Unlike GDB, Blinkenlights focuses on visualizing program execution.
fetch_log: https://github.com/jart/blink : fetched OK, returned the README (blinkenlights/blink combined README, about 40k characters before truncation). Did not follow further links; README was complete enough to write the brief.

judge.reason: Blink is a remarkably small cross-platform x86-64 Linux emulator, and its CP437 memory-visualizing debugger with reverse stepping makes execution tangible.

entry.title: blink
entry.tldr: A 221kb x86-64 Linux emulator for any POSIX host, with blinkenlights, a terminal debugger that animates memory as you step through assembly.
entry.deeper_look:
Blink is a user-mode emulator written in ANSI C11. It takes a Linux x86-64 ELF binary, or a Cosmopolitan Actually Portable Executable, and runs it on another POSIX system such as macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD or Cygwin. It does this by decoding the instructions itself and translating Linux system calls to the host. Hot code is JIT-compiled to native functions on x86_64 and aarch64.

The README pitches it as a smaller, more portable alternative to qemu-x86_64: about 221kb against a 4mb binary, and running on any POSIX system rather than only Linux. Decoding uses a trimmed-down version of Intel's Xed disassembler. Guest memory is virtualized through a four-level page table with a small TLB, or through a faster linear mapping.

The companion program, blinkenlights, is the reason to stop by. It is a terminal UI debugger that draws memory panels as IBM Code Page 437 glyphs, and the panels change as you single-step the assembly. You can also scroll the mouse wheel over the disassembly to run execution backward. In the README's words: "Unlike GDB, Blinkenlights focuses on visualizing program execution."

The larger idea is that a CPU is just a program you can read. Because the whole emulator is small, you can follow how instructions, memory and syscalls fit together, and then watch a real binary do it.
entry.install:
brew install blink
# The README builds from source (needs a C11 compiler and a modern GNU Make). The TUI needs a UTF-8 VT100/xterm-style terminal such as kitty, GNOME Terminal or Terminal.app.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the version and build configuration, confirming the install works.
Opens the bundled hello-world binary in the debugger TUI so you can step through it and watch memory change. The file ships in the source repository.
Runs the same hello-world binary headless under the emulator, with no debugger.

entry.whats_unique: Most emulators are big and hide what they do. Blink is a few hundred kilobytes, runs on many hosts, and ships a debugger built around watching execution, with reverse stepping.
entry.caveats: Not every Linux program works: many address families and Linux-only syscalls return EINVAL, x87 long double is only 64-bit, and the README gives no maintenance dates.
